title: What is known about 1RB---_0RC0LA_1LD0RB_1LE0RF_1LF1LC_1LB0LD
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB---_0RC0LA_1LD0RB_1LE0RF_1LF1LC_1LB0LD.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The head bounces between the left end, where a block grows by one 6-cell word every two sweeps, and a chaotic wall in the middle that very slowly eats an older block; the wall never repeats and its long-term behaviour is unknown.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (A1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 54,647 cells have been visited and 36,972 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.58). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).

claims.title: A bouncer with a slowly eating wall
claims.text: At the left-end visits in state F the first block (110111)^n grows by one word every two sweeps (n = 34,521 at 1.9·1010 steps) and the block behind the wall goes from 1,461 to 1,455 words between 7·107 and 1.9·1010 steps; the wall takes 33,482 different forms in the 33,482 sweeps after 8·107 steps up to 5·109.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The decider pipeline of bbchallenge left it open; no proof either way is recorded here yet.

facts.text: words of the old block eaten by the wall in 2·10<sup>10</sup> steps.
No halt in the C simulator; 54,647 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.

sections.heading: A growing block and a chaotic wall
html: The tape is the 6-cell word 110111 repeated, in a few long blocks. Each sweep, the head runs from the left end across the first block into a wall of a few dozen irregular cells, rewrites it and comes back. Every two sweeps the first block is one word longer.

Behind the wall lies an older block of about 1,460 words, which used to be the growing block until the wall jumped to the front at 6.9·107 steps. The wall eats it very slowly and irregularly: 1,461 words then, 1,455 after 1.9·1010 steps. The wall never takes the same form twice, so nothing like a finite-state argument applies; what happens when the old block is used up is unknown.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.58). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 54,647 cells (41,298 left of the start, 22 right), with a density of 1s of 0.677.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machines below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in any of the others, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

summary: A bouncer: the block at the left end grows by one word every two sweeps, and a chaotic, never-repeating wall in the middle eats the previous block (m = 1461 down to 1455 in 2·10^10 steps).
